In a 2013 study, Swiss researchers analyzed data from an experiment in which participants had no idea their sleep was being studied for lunar effects.

Australia’s tropical forests have become the world’s first to emit(排放) more carbon into the atmosphere than they are taking in, as a new study reports in Nature.

Surprisingly, the extra atmospheric carbon dioxide(CO₂) didn’t boost plant growth as climate models predicted, likely due to limited availability of nutrients plants need like phosphorus and other basic ones – a factor that must be considered in estimating the fate of forests.
Protecting these forests will require global financial investments to triple to $300 billion by 2030, yet global efforts for the protection are falling short of the intended commitments.
“Tropical forests are huge carbon reservoirs and we must cherish the forest carbon stocks already built up over centuries, or even millennia.” says the programme manager Wannes Hubau in the report.
“Losing them would be like setting off a carbon bomb, worsening climate change.”
They were turning into carbon emitters.
Tropical forests will die back by 2035.
